core: Equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity as the intersection of supply and demand where the market clears
Surplus (excess supply) at prices above equilibrium and the downward price pressure it creates
Shortage (excess demand) at prices below equilibrium and the upward price pressure it creates
The adjustment mechanism that moves a market from disequilibrium back to the clearing price
Comparative statics: how a shift in demand (one clear case) changes equilibrium price and quantity
A worked numeric example solving two linear equations for equilibrium, with arithmetic verified
supporting: Definitions of quantity demanded and quantity supplied as inputs to the equilibrium condition
Market clearing and disequilibrium as named states
outOfScope: Derivation of the demand and supply curves and the shift-vs-movement distinction (owned by the demand and supply topics; referenced only)
Binding price ceilings and floors and their welfare effects (owned by the price-controls topic; named as preventing equilibrium and handed off)
Elasticity and the responsiveness of quantity to price (separate topic)
Consumer surplus, producer surplus, and efficiency analysis

claims.claim: Market equilibrium is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, located where the supply and demand curves intersect; at that price the market clears.
When price is above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, producing a surplus (excess supply) that puts downward pressure on price.
When price is below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, producing a shortage (excess demand) that puts upward pressure on price.

A free market tends to move back toward equilibrium: a surplus leads sellers to cut prices and a shortage lets sellers raise prices, in each case closing the gap until quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

An increase in demand (a rightward shift) with supply unchanged raises both the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity; comparative statics analyzes such changes by comparing the old and new equilibria.

The same demand-and-supply equilibrium logic applies beyond goods markets; in a labor market the equilibrium wage is where quantity of labor supplied equals quantity demanded, with surpluses and shortages when the wage is off equilibrium.

For the linear model Qd = 100 - 4P and Qs = 20 + 4P, equilibrium is P = 10 and Q = 60; at P = 12 there is a surplus of 16 and at P = 8 a shortage of 16; increasing demand to Qd = 140 - 4P moves equilibrium to P = 15, Q = 80.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 3.1: Demand, Supply, and Equilibrium in Markets for Goods and Services
sourceRecords.notes: Primary source for the equilibrium definitions (equilibrium, equilibrium price, equilibrium quantity), surplus/shortage as excess supply/demand, and the adjustment mechanism. Chapter 3 key-terms page corroborated the exact term definitions. The book's gasoline example (equilibrium $1.40/600 million gallons; surplus and shortage at prices above/below) confirmed the mechanism direction; our lesson uses a different, independently computed linear example. License verified via web search as CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for the 3e edition; used as reference only with original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Chapter 4: Labor and Financial Markets
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the claim that the same demand-and-supply equilibrium framework extends to input markets. The chapter's Minneapolis-St. Paul nursing example shows an equilibrium wage where labor supply meets labor demand, with excess supply above and shortage below the equilibrium wage. Used to justify the breadth claim only; no wording reproduced.
